paras: The beating of Benjamin Herne was an assault in Atlanta, Georgia, in early May 1919, in which a white drug-store clerk named Powell struck Herne, a Black soldier recently returned from France, on the head with a baseball bat after Herne asked for a drink at the store's soda fountain. Herne was carried insensible to Grady Hospital, and most reports said Powell was arrested for "disorderly conduct." The Associated Negro Press spread the story to Black papers across the country as a sign of how returned Black soldiers were treated in the South, and a Macon newspaper's defense of the beating drew a reply from the Chicago Defender.

The dispatch opened by saying it was "more and more apparent from day to day" that a "show down" for "equal rights" and a "consequent clash of races" would follow if those rights were not granted. It quoted a Macon daily that had noticed for several weeks, on street cars, in railway stations and in other public places in Atlanta, a "marked difference" in the bearing toward white people of Black soldiers back from abroad.

According to the dispatch, Herne went into a drug store to make some purchases and, on his way out, stopped at the soda fountain and asked for a drink. Powell, described as a white clerk, took a bat from beneath the counter and pounded Herne on the head with it. Herne was picked up insensible, taken to Grady Hospital, and later returned to his quarters at Camp Gordon. No report gives the exact date; the earliest datelines on the dispatch read May 6.

Most printings of the dispatch said Powell was arrested for "disorderly conduct," a charge the Kansas City Sun placed in quotation marks as its headline. The Macon daily described the matter as "the first police court case" growing out of an attempt by returned Black soldiers "to force 'race equality.'" No report of how the court disposed of the case, or of Herne's recovery, appears in the coverage.

The Associated Negro Press account ran in Black weeklies from May 9 through May 30, including the Baltimore Afro-American, the Black Dispatch, the Cleveland Advocate, the Dallas Express, the Omaha Monitor, the Phoenix Tribune, the St. Louis Argus and the Metropolis Weekly Gazette. Its text was sardonic, saying Herne had forgotten he was in "the hate-clime of Georgia" rather than France, and editors gave it pointed headlines such as "Soldier Asks for Drink; Hoodlum Gives Him Club" in Cleveland and "How They Treat Our Returned Heroes In Dear Old Georgia" in Phoenix. The Cleveland Gazette ran a shortened version under "BEAT INSENSIBLE!" with the subheading "Still Leaving the South" and a report that Black migrants were not returning from the North.

White Georgia opinion reached Black readers through reprints of the Macon Telegraph's editorial "Georgia Sentiment on Racial Bounds." The editorial said neither war savings stamps, Liberty bonds nor the khaki uniform could excuse a "racial overstepping of bounds," that the soldier had justified himself by his uniform and his service in France, and that he "simply made a mistake." It added that "the drug store in Atlanta" and "the immediate community in Millen" would not suffer a repetition, and it insisted that "this is a white man's country."

The Chicago Defender quoted the Macon editorial on May 17 and answered it with sarcasm, writing that a baseball bat "might have its advantages" as a way of telling someone soda was not served at a fountain. The Defender asked whether "this a white man's country because a white man says so?" and warned that persecution might breed disloyalty an alien foe could exploit. The New York Age reprinted the Macon editorial on June 21 without comment, alongside other Southern white opinion pieces.

Accounts differ on who was arrested: most copies of the dispatch, including the cleanest texts, name Powell, while garbled versions in the Black Dispatch and Dallas Express say Herne was arrested for disorderly conduct. The Macon daily's description of the affair as a police court case over an attempt to force "race equality" leaves open whether Herne also appeared before the court.

reader.title: Beating of Benjamin Herne
bases: A single white drug-store clerk, Powell, was reported to have beaten a Black soldier with a bat after he asked for a drink at the soda fountain; no mob or crowd took part (A3, A6, A13).

The Associated Negro Press dispatch (A1, A3, A6) and the Macon Telegraph editorial reprinted and quoted in the Black press (A7, A13) agree that a Black soldier who asked for service at a white soda fountain in Atlanta was struck on the head with a baseball bat, though the dispatch itself drew on Georgia daily reports.

accounts.label: Associated Negro Press dispatch
accounts.gist: Herne stopped at a drug-store soda fountain and asked for a drink; Powell, a white clerk, beat him on the head with a bat, and Powell was arrested for 'disorderly conduct'.

accounts.label: Macon daily (quoted in the dispatch)
accounts.gist: Called it the first police court case growing out of an attempt by returned Black soldiers to force 'race equality', and described a change in the bearing of Black soldiers back from abroad.

accounts.label: Macon Telegraph editorial (reprinted)
accounts.gist: Said a Black man sought equal service at a 'white man's' soda fountain, justified himself by his uniform and service in France, and 'simply made a mistake'; the drug store would not suffer a repetition.

framing.detail: The ANP dispatch mocked the 'hate-clime of Georgia' and headlines such as 'Soldier Asks for Drink; Hoodlum Gives Him Club' and 'FORGOT HE WAS NOT IN DEMOCRATIC FRANCE' set the beating against the soldier's war service.
The Chicago Defender quoted the Macon editorial and answered it, asking whether this was a white man's country 'because a white man says so'.
The New York Age reprinted the Macon Telegraph's justification of the beating, without comment, as an example of Southern white opinion.

versions.value: Powell, the clerk, was arrested for 'disorderly conduct'.
Herne, the soldier, was arrested for disorderly conduct.

conflicts.note: Most copies, including the cleanest texts, name Powell; the two that name Herne are badly garbled at that point. The Macon daily's phrase 'police court case' arising from an attempt to force 'race equality' and the Macon Telegraph's remark that the soldier justified himself 'by his own declaration' leave open that Herne also faced the court.
The same editorial's continuation says 'the drug store in Atlanta' and the Chicago Defender's quotation of it reads Atlanta, so 'Athens' is most likely an OCR error.
